what_it_does: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are implanted devices that read electrical signals from neurons and translate them into commands; because brain signals drift over time, the AI model inside the device must keep learning and updating itself — a process called continual learning. Implantable chips cannot use ordinary volatile memory (which loses data when power is cut) because they may experience brief power interruptions; they rely on non-volatile memory (NVM — memory that retains data without power, similar in concept to flash storage). Writing to NVM is expensive: each write consumes energy and physically wears out the memory cells, meaning too many writes shortens the device's life. InfiniMind adds a layer of smarts to the memory controller (the circuit that manages reads and writes) with four tricks: filtering out redundant writes when the neural signal hasn't meaningfully changed; accumulating small incremental changes in a temporary buffer and writing them out in one larger batch; packing multiple small updates into a single physical write operation; and compressing neural waveforms before storing them. Together these reduce how often and how much is written to NVM, making the implant last far longer.
